# Introduction and research question

Instrumental temperature records that begin in the eighteenth century
are among the longest direct observations of near-surface climate.
Estimating a trend from such a record requires more than fitting a
straight line: residual autocorrelation, changing variance and changes
in the trend itself all affect which statistical conclusions are valid.
This report analyses the annual mean temperature record of Geneva
(Station08) and addresses the question: *what does this record reveal
about long-term warming, about the adequacy of a single linear trend,
and about a possible change in the trend at an unknown date?*

Section 2 describes the data and their gap structure. Section 3
estimates a linear trend and examines its residuals, including a Monte
Carlo Durbin–Watson test and a Breusch–Pagan test. Section 4 fits a
continuous broken-trend model with an unknown break date, tests for the
break with bootstrap procedures chosen in light of the Section 3
diagnostics, and constructs bootstrap confidence intervals for the pre-
and post-break slopes. Section 5 evaluates the finite-sample size and
power of these bootstrap procedures by simulation, and Section 6
concludes. All numbers quoted in the text are computed by the embedded
code; executable consistency checks are collected in Appendix A.

# Data and exploratory analysis

## Station, data source and sample

The series is the Geneva station (Switzerland; 46.20°N, 6.15°E;
elevation 405 m) from the Global Historical Climatology Network Monthly
Temperature dataset, version 4, of the NOAA National Centers for
Environmental Information (GHCN-M v4; Menne et al., 2018; DOI
10.7289/V5XW4GTH). Annual means are formed only for years with at least
ten valid monthly values; the supplied file contains the calendar year
and the annual mean temperature in °C.

We use the QCF series, i.e. the quality-controlled and
homogenisation-adjusted version. This matters for interpretation. The
pairwise homogenisation applied in GHCN-M v4 is designed to remove
artificial level shifts caused by, for example, station relocations or
instrument changes, so a change in trend detected in this series is less
likely to be a documented measurement artefact. Adjustments for the
earliest decades, however, rest on few neighbouring stations, and
residual inhomogeneities cannot be ruled out with the information
supplied.

The file contains 226 annual observations between 1753 and 2013. Since
261 calendar years lie in this range, 35 years are missing; they are
located below. Apart from sorting by year and validating the file, no
transformation is applied to the temperatures. The only transformation
of the time variable is the rescaled index defined in Section 2.2.

```{r load-data}
master_seed <- 20260926L
set.seed(master_seed)

library(ggplot2)

dat <- read.csv(file.path(project_root, "Station08.csv"))
stopifnot(identical(names(dat), c("Year", "Temperature")),
          nrow(dat) == 226L, !anyNA(dat),
          all(is.finite(dat$Year)), all(is.finite(dat$Temperature)),
          !anyDuplicated(dat$Year))

# Sort by year, validate supplied data instead of silently dropping observations.
dat <- dat[order(dat$Year), ]
stopifnot(all(diff(dat$Year)>0))
n <- nrow(dat)

cat("Number of observations n =", n, "\n")
cat("First year:", min(dat$Year), " Last year:", max(dat$Year), "\n")
```

## Gap structure and time index

```{r gap-detection}
# ---- Gap diagnostics: locate every "year jump" ----
full_years     <- seq(min(dat$Year), max(dat$Year))
missing_years  <- setdiff(full_years, dat$Year)
# year difference between consecutive observations
gap_len        <- diff(dat$Year)
# a difference > 1 indicates a gap
gap_start_idx  <- which(gap_len > 1)

gap_table <- data.frame(
  from      = dat$Year[gap_start_idx],
  to        = dat$Year[gap_start_idx + 1],
  n_missing = gap_len[gap_start_idx] - 1
)

print(gap_table)
cat("\nTotal missing years:", length(missing_years), "\n")
cat("Number of gaps:", nrow(gap_table), "\n")
big_gap <- gap_table[which.max(gap_table$n_missing), ]
cat("Largest gap:", big_gap$n_missing, "years, from", big_gap$from, "to", big_gap$to, "\n")
```

The record contains `r nrow(gap_table)` gaps with a total of
`r length(missing_years)` missing years. Four gaps are short (one to
three years) and lie between 1931 and 1979. The fifth spans
`r big_gap$from + 1`–`r big_gap$to - 1`, i.e. `r big_gap$n_missing`
consecutive years, and separates the last four observations (2010–2013)
from the rest of the record. Observations that are adjacent in the data
file are therefore not always adjacent in calendar time. We keep every
supplied observation, use the actual calendar year as time regressor,
and state for each diagnostic whether lags are counted in observation
positions or in calendar years. In all time-series figures, lines
connect only observations within the same run of consecutive years, so
no line suggests data inside a gap.

**Time index.** The time regressor is
$$t_i = (\mathrm{Year}_i - 1850)/10 .$$ Dividing by ten expresses every
slope in °C per decade. Centring at 1850 places the reference year next
to the break date estimated in Section 4, which lies in the
mid-nineteenth century. As a result, the intercept of the linear model
is its fitted temperature in 1850, and the intercept of the broken-trend
model is also its fitted temperature in 1850, since the estimated break
occurs after this reference year. The two intercepts are therefore directly
comparable at the same reference year. Centring is a reparametrisation:
it changes only the intercept and leaves fitted values, residuals,
slopes and every test statistic unchanged (Appendix C; verified
numerically in Appendix A). The reference year was chosen after seeing
the Section 4 estimate; it serves presentation only and carries no
inferential weight.

```{r segment-and-t}
# Increment the segment id by 1 whenever the year jumps by more than 1 year; used to avoid drawing lines across gaps
dat$segment <- c(1, cumsum(diff(dat$Year) > 1) + 1)

# Centered, decade-scaled time index
dat$t <- (dat$Year - 1850) / 10
```

## Exploratory analysis

```{r explore-plot, fig.width=8, fig.height=4.5, fig.cap="Annual mean temperature at Geneva, 1753–2013 (°C). Lines connect consecutive years only; the shaded band marks the 1981–2009 period without observations."}
ggplot(dat, aes(x = Year, y = Temperature)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = big_gap$from, xmax = big_gap$to,
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = gap_fill) +
  geom_line(aes(group = segment), linewidth = 0.4, colour = gray_line) +
  geom_point(size = 0.8, colour = gray) +
  labs(
    title = "Station08 annual mean temperature (1753-2013)",
    subtitle = "Grey shading = largest data gap (1981-2009, no observations)",
    x = "Year", y = "Annual mean temperature (°C)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(text = element_text(colour = label_colour),
        axis.text = element_text(colour = axis_colour))
```

```{r explore-stats}
cat("Temperature range:", round(range(dat$Temperature), 2), "\n")
cat("5 coldest years:\n")
print(head(dat[order(dat$Temperature), c("Year", "Temperature")], 5))
cat("5 warmest years:\n")
print(tail(dat[order(dat$Temperature), c("Year", "Temperature")], 5))
cat("Standard deviation before 1900:", round(sd(dat$Temperature[dat$Year < 1900]), 3),
    "  Standard deviation from 1900 onward:", round(sd(dat$Temperature[dat$Year >= 1900]), 3), "\n")
```

The figure above shows the series. Its main empirical features are the
following.

**Direction of the trend.** The record does not rise uniformly. Mean
temperature is `r fmt(mean(dat$Temperature[dat$Year < 1800]), 2)` °C
before 1800,
`r fmt(mean(dat$Temperature[dat$Year >= 1800 & dat$Year < 1850]), 2)` °C
in 1800–1849,
`r fmt(mean(dat$Temperature[dat$Year >= 1850 & dat$Year < 1900]), 2)` °C
in 1850–1899 and
`r fmt(mean(dat$Temperature[dat$Year >= 1900 & dat$Year <= 1980]), 2)`
°C in 1900–1980. The series thus drifts downward from the late
eighteenth into the mid-nineteenth century and rises mainly during the
twentieth century. All four observations after the long gap rank among
the twelve warmest years of the record. A single straight line through
this record averages an early flat-to-cooling phase with later warming,
which motivates the broken-trend analysis of Section 4.

**Interannual variability.** The sample standard deviation is
`r fmt(sd(dat$Temperature), 2)` °C, and year-to-year changes are large
relative to the long-run movements described above. The standard
deviation is `r fmt(sd(dat$Temperature[dat$Year < 1900]), 3)` °C before
1900 and `r fmt(sd(dat$Temperature[dat$Year >= 1900]), 3)` °C from 1900
onwards. These raw figures also contain trend movements within each
sub-period, so they indicate only that variability has not visibly
increased; Section 3 assesses changing variance formally.

**Unusual observations.** The coldest year is
`r dat$Year[which.min(dat$Temperature)]`
(`r fmt(min(dat$Temperature), 2)` °C) and the warmest is
`r dat$Year[which.max(dat$Temperature)]`
(`r fmt(max(dat$Temperature), 2)` °C). No observation is removed. The
coldest year lies in the same period as the break date estimated in
Section 4, which therefore checks how sensitive the estimated break is
to this single year.

**Missing decades.** The 2010–2013 observations follow 29 years without
data. They cannot show whether warming during that interval was gradual,
accelerating or interrupted, and we do not interpret the difference
between 1980 and 2010 as a discontinuity.

# Linear trend and model diagnostics

We first examine whether a single linear trend is an adequate initial
description of the series. This section concentrates on estimation,
interpretation and diagnostics; the statistical significance of the
trend is not assessed here. The model is
$$y_i=\beta_0 + \beta_1 t_i + \varepsilon_i, \qquad i=1,\ldots,n,$$
where $y_i$ is the annual mean temperature of the $i$-th observation,
$i$ indexes observation positions, and $t_i=(\mathrm{Year}_i-1850)/10$
is the calendar-time index of Section 2.2. Hence $\beta_0$ is the fitted
temperature in 1850 and $\beta_1$ is the trend in °C per decade.

## OLS estimation of the linear trend

```{r ols-fit}
trend_model <- lm(Temperature ~ t, data = dat)
summary(trend_model)

print(coef(trend_model))
cat("R-squared:", round(summary(trend_model)$r.squared, 4), "\n")

beta0_hat <- coef(trend_model)[1]
beta1_hat <- coef(trend_model)[2]

cat("Estimated intercept (fitted temperature in 1850):", round(beta0_hat, 3), "°C\n")
cat("Estimated slope:", round(beta1_hat, 4), "°C per decade\n")
cat("Converted to per century:", round(beta1_hat * 10, 3), "°C per century\n")

```

```{r ols-plot, fig.width=8, fig.height=4.5, fig.cap="Annual mean temperature (grey) with the OLS linear trend (navy), °C. The shaded band marks the 1981–2009 gap."}
dat$fitted_linear <- fitted(trend_model)

ggplot(dat, aes(x = Year, y = Temperature)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = big_gap$from, xmax = big_gap$to,
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = gap_fill) +
  geom_line(aes(group = segment), linewidth = 0.4, colour = gray_line) +
  geom_point(size = 0.8, colour = gray) +
  geom_line(aes(y = fitted_linear), colour = navy, linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Geneva temperature series with OLS linear trend",
       x = "Year", y = "Annual mean temperature (°C)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(text = element_text(colour = label_colour),
        axis.text = element_text(colour = axis_colour))
```

**Interpretation.** The estimated intercept, $\hat\beta_0=$
`r fmt(beta0_hat, 3)` °C, is the temperature implied by the fitted line
in 1850. The estimated slope, $\hat\beta_1=$ `r fmt(beta1_hat, 4)` °C
per decade (`r fmt(10 * beta1_hat, 3)` °C per century), is the average
linear change over the observed record. The trend explains only a small
share of the total variation ($R^2=$
`r fmt(summary(trend_model)$r.squared, 3)`), consistent with the
exploratory finding that interannual variability dominates the long-run
change.

**Effect of the gaps.** Because the regressor is calendar time, the
slope keeps its meaning under unequal spacing, and OLS is well defined
for this fixed design. The gaps nevertheless determine which periods are
represented and therefore affect the estimate and its precision. The
`r sum(dat$Year <= 1980)` observations up to 1980 inform the slope as
well; it is not determined solely by a contrast between the four
post-gap values and the rest. A single slope says nothing about the path
of temperature inside the missing decades, and neither the exogeneity of
the errors nor the mechanism behind the missing years can be verified
from the supplied file. In line with the research design, no
significance statement about $\beta_1$ is made at this stage.

## Residual diagnostics

```{r residuals}
dat$residual    <- residuals(trend_model)
dat$residual_sq <- dat$residual^2
```

### Residuals over time

```{r resid-time-plot, fig.width=8, fig.height=4.5, fig.cap="Residuals of the linear trend model against calendar year (°C). Lines connect consecutive years only; the shaded band marks the 1981–2009 gap."}
ggplot(dat, aes(x = Year, y = residual)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = big_gap$from, xmax = big_gap$to,
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = gap_fill) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = navy) +
  geom_line(aes(group = segment), linewidth = 0.4, colour = gray_line) +
  geom_point(size = 0.8, colour = gray) +
  labs(title = "Residuals from the linear trend model", x = "Year", y = "Residual (°C)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(text = element_text(colour = label_colour),
        axis.text = element_text(colour = axis_colour))
```

The residuals fluctuate around zero, with runs of similarly signed
values and low-frequency departures from the linear fit. These patterns
suggest residual dependence and possible inadequacy of the
constant-trend mean. We inspect both observation-lag and calendar-lag
ACFs, then calibrate the Durbin–Watson statistic by Monte Carlo
simulation.

### Residual autocorrelation by observation and calendar lag

**Why the lag definition matters:** Applied to the observed residual
vector, `acf()` measures lag by row position. It is a valid description
of dependence between observed rows, but a one-observation lag is not
always a one-calendar-year lag. For example, observations
`r match(1980, dat$Year)` and `r match(2010, dat$Year)` correspond to
1980 and 2010, thirty calendar years apart.

**Calendar-lag comparison:** Place residuals on the full calendar grid,
insert `NA` for unobserved years, and use `na.action = na.pass`. This
uses available pairs for each calendar lag without imputing
temperatures. With missing values, the resulting estimates need not
define a valid autocorrelation sequence; the usual plot bounds are
descriptive rather than calibrated inference. Both ACFs are retained,
and their lag meanings are stated explicitly.

```{r acf-compare, fig.width=9, fig.height=4, fig.cap="Sample autocorrelation of the linear-trend residuals by observation lag (left) and by calendar-year lag with missing years set to NA (right)."}
# Naive approach (uncorrected, shown only for comparison to illustrate the problem)
acf_naive <- acf(dat$residual, lag.max = 20, plot = FALSE)

# Corrected approach: place back on the full calendar grid + na.action = na.pass
res_full <- rep(NA_real_, length(full_years))
res_full[match(dat$Year, full_years)] <- dat$residual
res_ts   <- ts(res_full, start = min(full_years), frequency = 1)
acf_gap  <- acf(res_ts, na.action = na.pass, lag.max = 20, plot = FALSE)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), col.axis = axis_colour, col.lab = label_colour,
    col.main = label_colour)
plot(acf_naive, main = "ACF by observation lag", col = navy, ci.col = teal)
plot(acf_gap,   main = "ACF by calendar-year lag", col = navy, ci.col = teal)

cat("Observation-lag 1 autocorrelation:", round(acf_naive$acf[2], 3), "\n")
cat("Calendar-lag 1 autocorrelation:", round(acf_gap$acf[2], 3), "\n")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

```

The first observation-lag and calendar-lag autocorrelations are
`r fmt(as.numeric(acf_naive$acf[2]), 3)` and
`r fmt(as.numeric(acf_gap$acf[2]), 3)`. They are close here because most
observed pairs are consecutive calendar years. Both indicate positive
short-range residual dependence. Their similarity in this dataset does
not make the two lag definitions interchangeable in general.

### Residual variance over time

```{r variance-plot, fig.width=8, fig.height=4.5, fig.cap="Squared residuals of the linear trend model (°C²) against calendar year, with a descriptive loess smooth. The shaded band marks the 1981–2009 gap."}
ggplot(dat, aes(x = Year, y = residual_sq)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = big_gap$from, xmax = big_gap$to,
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = gap_fill) +
  geom_point(size = 0.8, colour = gray) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, colour = teal) +
  labs(
    title = "Squared residuals over time",
    subtitle = "Caution: the smooth line is not supported by any observations inside the shaded region",
    x = "Year", y = expression(hat(epsilon)[t]^2)
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(text = element_text(colour = label_colour),
        axis.text = element_text(colour = axis_colour))
```

The scatter uses actual calendar years. The loess curve is a descriptive
smooth, and its portion inside the long gap is not supported by
observations from those years. The final four observations can influence
its endpoint behavior; the plot cannot establish how variance evolved
during the gap. No formal conclusion about constant variance follows
from this smooth alone.

### Normal QQ plot

```{r qq-plot, fig.width=5, fig.height=5, fig.cap="Normal QQ plot of the linear-trend residuals (°C)."}
par(col.axis = axis_colour, col.lab = label_colour, col.main = label_colour)
qqnorm(dat$residual, main = "Normal QQ plot of residuals", col = gray)
qqline(dat$residual, col = teal)
```

The QQ plot is broadly linear in its center, with some tail departures.
This is compatible with a Gaussian approximation but does not verify
normality. Time spacing does not enter the QQ construction, although the
plotted marginal distribution still reflects only the observed years.
Gaussian errors remain an explicit reference assumption for the DW Monte
Carlo calibration.

## Monte Carlo Durbin–Watson test for first-order autocorrelation

**Primary statistic.** The research design specifies the Durbin–Watson
statistic.

$$d=\frac{\sum_{i=2}^n(\widehat e_i-\widehat e_{i-1})^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n\widehat e_i^2}.$$

Adjacency in its numerator is by observation position. We implement this
definition as the primary test and interpret it accordingly. Calendar
gaps affect its meaning, but restricting the numerator to
calendar-adjacent pairs would define a different statistic rather than
implement the specified one.

**Calendar-adjacency sensitivity.** As a sensitivity check we also
compute

$$d_{\mathrm{calendar}}=\frac{\sum_{i:\ s_{i+1}-s_i=1}(\widehat e_{i+1}-\widehat e_i)^2}{\sum_i\widehat e_i^2},$$

where $s_i$ is the calendar year of observation $i$. It uses only pairs
of genuinely consecutive years. Both statistics can be written as
$e'Ae/e'e$ with different difference matrices $A$, and each is
calibrated with its own formula under the same observed regression
design.

```{r dw-define}
# Naive DW (uncorrected, shown only for comparison)
dw_naive_stat <- function(e) sum(diff(e)^2) / sum(e^2)
d_obs_naive <- dw_naive_stat(dat$residual)

# ---- Gap-sensitive DW: only compute differences over pairs that are truly calendar-adjacent (year difference = 1) ----
valid_pairs <- which(diff(dat$Year) == 1)      # indices of valid "adjacent pairs"
m_pairs <- length(valid_pairs)

Dmat <- matrix(0, nrow = m_pairs, ncol = n)
for (k in seq_len(m_pairs)) {
  i <- valid_pairs[k]
  Dmat[k, i]     <- -1
  Dmat[k, i + 1] <-  1
}
A_gap <- crossprod(Dmat)   # A = D'D

dw_gap_stat <- function(e) as.numeric((t(e) %*% A_gap %*% e) / (t(e) %*% e))
d_obs_gap <- dw_gap_stat(dat$residual)
d_obs <- d_obs_naive  # primary statistic: assignment definition

cat("Assigned observation-adjacency DW:", round(d_obs_naive, 4), "\n")
cat("Gap-sensitive DW statistic:", round(d_obs_gap, 4), "\n")
cat("Valid calendar-adjacent year pairs used:", m_pairs, "/", n - 1, "sequence-adjacent pairs\n")

```

The primary statistic is `r fmt(d_obs)`, and the calendar-adjacency
variant is `r fmt(d_obs_gap)`. There are `r m_pairs` calendar-adjacent
pairs among the `r n-1` observation-adjacent pairs. Both are reported;
the primary statistic governs the conclusion of this section.

### Design of the Monte Carlo test

Under the null hypothesis $\varepsilon\sim N(0,\sigma^2 I_n)$, the OLS
residuals are $e=M_X\varepsilon$ with $M_X=I-X(X'X)^{-1}X'$. The
projection removes the regression coefficients, and because $d=e'Ae/e'e$
is a ratio of quadratic forms in $e$, the error variance cancels. The
null distribution of $d$ therefore depends only on the known design
matrix $X$ and the difference matrix $A$: $d$ is *pivotal* under this
null, and its exact finite-sample distribution can be simulated to any
desired precision.

The test proceeds as follows. For $b=1,\ldots,B$ with $B=9{,}999$, draw
$\varepsilon^{*}_b\sim N(0,I_n)$, form $e^*_b=M_X\varepsilon^*_b$, and
evaluate both DW definitions on $e^*_b$. Because the null distribution
of $d$ need not be symmetric around two, the two tails are calibrated
separately: the lower and upper critical values $c_L$ and $c_U$ are the
empirical 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles of the simulated statistics (R's
type-6 quantile), not one quantile reflected around two. The **rejection
region** of the two-sided 5% test is therefore
$$\mathcal R=\{d<c_L\}\cup\{d>c_U\},$$ two tails that need not be
equally far from two. Values in the lower tail indicate positive
first-order autocorrelation; values in the upper tail indicate negative
autocorrelation. The two-sided Monte Carlo p-value is
$$p=\min\Bigl\{1,\;2\min\Bigl(\tfrac{1+\#\{d^*_b\le d\}}{B+1},\;\tfrac{1+\#\{d^*_b\ge d\}}{B+1}\Bigr)\Bigr\}.$$
With $B=9{,}999$, the type-6 cutoffs are the 250th and 9,750th ordered
simulated statistics. Under the continuous null, strict rejection
outside these cutoffs agrees with $p\le0.05$. This rank rule has exact
5% size under the iid Gaussian null, although the simulated cutoffs and
p-value vary across simulation runs. It is not a test of the broader
null of every process without first-order correlation, and non-Gaussian errors would
change the reference distribution.

```{r dw-mc-test}
X <- model.matrix(trend_model)
H <- X %*% solve(t(X) %*% X) %*% t(X)
M <- diag(n) - H

set.seed(master_seed)
B <- 9999L
d_sim <- d_sim_gap <- numeric(B)

for (b in seq_len(B)) {
  eps_star <- rnorm(n)
  e_star <- as.numeric(M %*% eps_star)
  d_sim[b] <- dw_naive_stat(e_star)   # assigned observation-adjacency statistic
  d_sim_gap[b] <- dw_gap_stat(e_star) # retained calendar-adjacent sensitivity
}

alpha <- 0.05
crit_lower <- unname(quantile(d_sim, alpha / 2, type = 6))
crit_upper <- unname(quantile(d_sim, 1 - alpha / 2, type = 6))
p_lower_adj <- (sum(d_sim <= d_obs) + 1) / (B + 1)
p_upper_adj <- (sum(d_sim >= d_obs) + 1) / (B + 1)
p_val_dw <- min(1, 2 * min(p_lower_adj, p_upper_adj))

crit_gap <- unname(quantile(d_sim_gap, c(alpha / 2, 1 - alpha / 2), type = 6))
p_val_dw_gap <- min(1, 2 * min(
  (sum(d_sim_gap <= d_obs_gap) + 1) / (B + 1),
  (sum(d_sim_gap >= d_obs_gap) + 1) / (B + 1)
))
dw_results <- data.frame(
  Definition = c("Assigned: observation adjacency", "Sensitivity: calendar adjacency"),
  Statistic = c(d_obs, d_obs_gap),
  Lower_2_5_percent = c(crit_lower, crit_gap[1]),
  Upper_97_5_percent = c(crit_upper, crit_gap[2]),
  Equal_tail_p_value = c(p_val_dw, p_val_dw_gap)
)
knitr::kable(dw_results, digits = 4)

# Optional packaged cross-check uses its own statistic/reference and is not the primary calibration.
if (requireNamespace("lmtest", quietly = TRUE)) {
  print(lmtest::dwtest(trend_model, alternative = "two.sided"))
}

```

**Result.** The observed statistic is $d=$ `r fmt(d_obs)`, with Monte
Carlo critical values $c_L=$ `r fmt(crit_lower)` and $c_U=$
`r fmt(crit_upper)` and two-sided p-value `r fmt(p_val_dw)`.
`r if (d_obs < crit_lower) "The statistic lies in the lower tail of the rejection region, so the null of no first-order autocorrelation is rejected at the 5% level in the direction of positive autocorrelation." else if (d_obs > crit_upper) "The statistic lies in the upper tail of the rejection region, so the null is rejected at the 5% level in the direction of negative autocorrelation." else "The statistic lies between the two critical values, so the null is not rejected at the 5% level."`
The calendar-adjacency variant gives p = `r fmt(p_val_dw_gap)`
`r if (p_val_dw_gap <= 0.05 && d_obs_gap < crit_gap[1]) "and also indicates positive dependence" else if (p_val_dw_gap <= 0.05) "and also rejects" else "and does not reject"`.
These results agree with the residual plot and both ACFs. A rejection
means that the independent Gaussian errors of the linear model are not
supported; it does not identify the cause, and a misspecified mean, such
as an unmodelled change in slope, can also produce autocorrelated
residuals.

## Breusch–Pagan test for heteroskedasticity

The auxiliary regression

$$\widehat e_i^2=\gamma_0+\gamma_1t_i+v_i$$

tests for a **linear variance trend**, using the requested statistic
$BP=nR^2$ and nominal $\chi^2_1$ reference. A zero time coefficient is a
narrow diagnostic null; non-rejection does not establish
homoskedasticity against every possible variance pattern.

**On gaps and calibration:** The regression uses actual transformed
calendar year and does not require equally spaced rows for its algebra.
Missing periods still limit interpretation, and the detected residual
dependence weakens the usual asymptotic chi-square reference. This
limitation is separate from the choice of observation versus calendar
adjacency in DW and ACF.

```{r bp-test}
aux_model <- lm(residual_sq ~ t, data = dat)
R2_aux   <- summary(aux_model)$r.squared
BP_stat  <- n * R2_aux
p_val_bp <- pchisq(BP_stat, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)

cat("Breusch-Pagan statistic BP:", round(BP_stat, 4), "\n")
cat("Degrees of freedom:", 1, "\n")
cat("BP p-value:", round(p_val_bp, 4), "\n")

# Previous cross-check: bptest(trend_model, varformula = ~ t, data = dat)
# Optional cross-check; no dependency on lmtest for the main result.
if (requireNamespace("lmtest", quietly = TRUE)) {
  print(lmtest::bptest(trend_model, varformula = ~ t, data = dat))
}

```

**Result.** $BP=$ `r fmt(BP_stat)` with nominal $\chi^2_1$ p-value
`r fmt(p_val_bp)`.
`r if (p_val_bp > 0.05) "Homoskedasticity is not rejected at the 5% level: there is no evidence of a linear trend in the residual variance." else "Homoskedasticity is rejected at the 5% level in favour of a linear trend in the residual variance."`
This is consistent with the variance plot. Non-rejection does not
establish constant variance, because the test is directed at one
specific alternative and its asymptotic reference distribution is
affected by the residual dependence found above.

## Comparing the inferential principles

A Monte Carlo test requires a statistic whose null distribution can be
simulated without knowing any unknown parameter, i.e. a statistic that
is pivotal under the null hypothesis being tested.

**Durbin–Watson.** The null hypothesis is fully specified up to
$(\beta,\sigma^2)$: independent $N(0,\sigma^2)$ errors. As shown above,
$\beta$ disappears through the projection $M_X$ and $\sigma^2$ cancels
in the ratio $e'Ae/e'e$. The null distribution of $d$ is therefore the
same for every admissible parameter value and depends only on the known
$X$. Simulating standard-normal errors reproduces it, and the Monte
Carlo rank test has exact 5% size for the replication count and rejection
rule used here (Dufour and Khalaf, 2001). This exactness is conditional
on normality: if the errors were independent but non-Gaussian, the simulated reference distribution would
only be an approximation.

**Breusch–Pagan.** The null of interest is homoskedasticity,
$\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_i)=\sigma^2$ for all $i$, and it does
not specify the error distribution. The statistic $BP=nR^2$ is
scale-invariant, so $\sigma^2$ still cancels. Its finite-sample
distribution, however, depends on the shape of the error distribution,
in particular on its kurtosis, because the auxiliary regression is
fitted to squared residuals whose variability is governed by the fourth
moment. The kurtosis is a nuisance parameter left unrestricted by the
homoskedasticity null, so $BP$ is not pivotal under that null. One could
simulate $BP$ under iid Gaussian errors, giving a finite-sample reference
distribution for that specific null. Applying those critical values to
homoskedastic errors with other distributions or serial dependence can
distort size. The $nR^2$ form used here is Koenker's
(1981) studentised version of the Breusch and Pagan (1979) test, whose
*asymptotic* $\chi^2_1$ distribution holds without normality; this is
why the test relies on the asymptotic reference rather than on a
simulated finite-sample distribution.

We therefore retain the asymptotic calibration and qualify its
conclusion in light of the residual dependence, rather than treating
non-rejection as proof of constant variance.

## Overall assessment of the initial model

Bringing the graphical and formal diagnostics together:

1.  **Positive descriptive slope.** The full-sample linear estimate is
    `r fmt(beta1_hat)` °C per decade, with $R^2=$
    `r fmt(summary(trend_model)$r.squared, 3)`. This is a modest average
    fitted change, not a statement about statistical significance.
2.  **Gaussian reference remains an assumption.** The QQ plot is broadly
    linear in its centre with tail departures; it does not verify
    normality.
3.  **No detected linear variance trend.** The nominal BP p-value is
    `r fmt(p_val_bp)`. Non-rejection does not establish
    homoskedasticity, and dependence qualifies the reference
    distribution.
4.  **Residual dependence matters.** Both DW variants and both ACFs
    indicate positive residual dependence. Conventional OLS standard
    errors that assume independent errors are therefore not a reliable
    basis for inference. A richer mean specification may reduce, but
    need not eliminate, this pattern.
5.  **Missing periods constrain interpretation.** Actual calendar
    spacing is retained, but there is no direct evidence about
    temperatures during 1981–2009, and the missingness mechanism and
    detailed station history are unknown.

**Conclusion.** The linear model is a useful starting description but
not an adequate final one. Its residual patterns motivate a model in
which the slope may change, and the detected dependence requires
inference that does not assume independent errors. Sections 4 and 5
carry out that inference and evaluate its finite-sample behaviour.

# Structural change and bootstrap inference

This section asks whether the temperature trend changed at an unknown
date. We fit a continuous broken-trend model, estimate the break date by
least squares over a trimmed set of candidate dates, test the no-break
null with bootstrap procedures selected on the basis of the Section 3
diagnostics, and construct bootstrap confidence intervals for the pre-
and post-break slopes.

```{r part2-setup}
year <- dat$Year
y <- dat$Temperature
x <- dat$t
m0 <- trend_model
e0 <- dat$residual
seed <- master_seed
B_test <- 9999L
B_ci <- 4999L
B_dw <- B
simulation_M <- 1000L
simulation_B <- 499L
dw <- d_obs
dwcrit <- c(crit_lower, crit_upper)
dwp<-p_val_dw
bp<- BP_stat
bpp <- p_val_bp
ncores<- parallel::detectCores()
if (is.na(ncores)) ncores <- 1L
stopifnot(is.logical(params$recompute_simulation),
          length(params$recompute_simulation) == 1L,
          !is.na(params$recompute_simulation),
          is.numeric(params$workers), length(params$workers) == 1L,
          is.finite(params$workers), params$workers >= 1)
workers <- min(as.integer(params$workers), ncores)
```

## Model, estimation and admissible break dates

**Model.** For a candidate break at observation $k$ we consider
$$y_i = \alpha + \beta x_i + \delta(x_i - x_k)_+ + \varepsilon_i, \qquad (z)_+=\max(0,z),$$
where $x_i$ is the decade-scaled time index. The hinge $(x_i-x_k)_+$ is
the regressor $D_{t,T_c}$ of the broken-trend model, measured in
decades. The model differs from the linear trend in three respects.
First, the slope is $\beta$ before the break and $\beta+\delta$ after
it, and the linear model is the special case $\delta=0$. Second, the
hinge equals zero at the break, so the fitted line is continuous: the
model allows a change in slope but no jump in level. Third, the break
date is an additional unknown parameter; the model is linear in
$(\alpha,\beta,\delta)$ but not in the break date.

**Estimation for a fixed date.** For a given candidate $k$, the hinge is
a known regressor. The model is then an ordinary linear regression of
$y$ on $[1,\ x,\ (x-x_k)_+]$, and $(\alpha,\beta,\delta)$ are estimated
by OLS, yielding $RSS(k)$. The break date is estimated by repeating this
for every admissible $k$ and choosing the candidate with the smallest
$RSS(k)$. This grid search is the least-squares estimator of the break
date.

**Admissible dates.** With trimming fraction $\lambda=0.15$, candidates
run from observation $\lceil 0.15n\rceil$ to $\lfloor 0.85n\rfloor$.
Trimming guarantees that each regime contains at least 15% of the
observations, so that both slopes are estimated from enough data and the
search is not dominated by fits to a few end points (Andrews, 1993). We
trim by observation position rather than by calendar span, because the
number of observations in each regime determines estimation precision.
Owing to the 1981–2009 gap, trimming 15% of the calendar span would
admit break dates with as few as eight observations after them.

**Computation.** For fast repeated searches, each candidate hinge is
residualised against $[1,x]$ and normalised to unit length. By the
Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem, the squared inner product of this vector
with the null residuals equals the reduction in RSS from adding the
hinge, so the whole search reduces to one matrix product. Appendix A
checks this against explicit OLS fits.

```{r prepare-break-design}
 prepare_design <- function(year,trim=0.15){
   stopifnot(is.numeric(year), all(is.finite(year)), length(year) >= 10L,
             all(diff(year)>0),
             length(trim)==1L, trim>0, trim<0.5)
   n<-length(year)
   x<-(year - mean(year))/10
   X0 <- cbind(intercept = 1, pre = x)
   qr0<- qr(X0)
   Q0 <- qr.Q(qr0)
   index<-seq.int(ceiling(trim*n), floor((1-trim)*n))
   H <- outer(x,x[index], function(a,b) pmax(0,a-b))
   Hres <- H - Q0 %*% crossprod(Q0,H)
   hnorm <- sqrt(colSums(Hres^2))
   stopifnot(all(hnorm>0))
   Qhinge<-sweep(Hres,2L, hnorm, "/")
   structure(list(year = year, n=n, x=x, X0=X0, qr0 = qr0, Q0=Q0, index=index, candidates=index, H=H, Qhinge=Qhinge, hinge_norm = hnorm, trim=trim), class = "break_design")
 }
```

The search function accepts a single series or a matrix of bootstrap
series, one per column. The test statistic is

$$F_T=RSS_0-\min_{k\in\mathcal K}RSS(k).$$

Despite its name, $F_T$ is the raw reduction in the residual sum of
squares (in °C²), not a variance-normalised F ratio. A normalised
version is also computed but not used for the reported tests. Ties are
resolved in favour of the earliest candidate.

```{r break-statistic-and-fit}
break_statistics <- function(y, design){
  if(is.null(dim(y))) y<-matrix(y, ncol = 1L)
  stopifnot(nrow(y) == design$n, all(is.finite(y)))
  resid0<-y-design$Q0 %*% crossprod(design$Q0,y)
  rss0 <- colSums(resid0^2)
  scores2 <- crossprod(design$Qhinge, resid0)^2
  best<- max.col(t(scores2), ties.method = "first")
  gain <- scores2[cbind(best, seq_len(ncol(y)))]
  rss1 <- pmax(rss0 - gain, .Machine$double.eps * pmax(rss0,1))
  list(F=gain, studentized_F = gain / (rss1/(design$n - 3L)),
  grid_index= best, RSS0 = rss0, RSS1= rss1, gain = gain)
}

fit_break <- function(y,design){
  stopifnot(is.numeric(y), length(y) == design$n, all(is.finite(y)))
  stats<- break_statistics(y,design)
  j<-stats$grid_index[1L]
  X1 <- cbind(design$X0, delta = design$H[, j])
  fit<- lm.fit(X1,y)
  co <- fit$coefficients
  co <- c(intercept = unname(co[1L]), pre=unname(co[2L]), delta = unname(co[3L]), 
          post = unname(co[2L] + co[3L]))
  null<- lm.fit(design$X0, y)
  list(F = unname(stats$F[1L]), index=design$index[j], year=design$year[design$index[j]], coef = co,
         pre = co[["pre"]], delta = co[["delta"]], post = co[["post"]],
       fitted = fit$fitted.values, residuals = fit$residuals,
       null_fitted = null$fitted.values, null_residuals = null$residuals,
       null_coef = null$coefficients, RSS0 = unname(stats$RSS0[1L]),
       RSS1 = unname(stats$RSS1[1L]))

}
```

```{r search-observed-break}
design <- prepare_design(year)
candidates<-design$index
# This explicit lm loop also provides an independent validation of the fast search.
rss<-sapply(candidates,function(k) sum(resid(lm(y~x+I(pmax(0,x-x[k]))))^2))
k<-candidates[which.min(rss)]; h<-pmax(0,x-x[k]); X1<-cbind(1,x,h)
m1<-lm(y~x+h); e1<-resid(m1); theta<-c(pre=coef(m1)[2],post=sum(coef(m1)[2:3]))
Fobs<-sum(e0^2)-min(rss)
fast<-fit_break(y,design)
stopifnot(abs(fast$F-Fobs)<1e-8)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  First_index = min(candidates), Last_index = max(candidates),
  First_year = year[min(candidates)], Last_year = year[max(candidates)],
  Selected_index = k, Selected_year = year[k],
  Linear_RSS = sum(e0^2), Broken_RSS = min(rss), Raw_RSS_reduction = Fobs
), digits = 4)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Parameter = c("Pre-break slope", "Slope change", "Post-break slope"),
  Estimate = c(unname(coef(m1)[2]), unname(coef(m1)[3]), unname(sum(coef(m1)[2:3])))
), digits = 4)
```

The search covers positions `r min(candidates)`–`r max(candidates)`,
i.e. the years `r year[min(candidates)]`–`r year[max(candidates)]`. The
minimum RSS is attained at $\widehat T_1=$ `r year[k]`, and the observed
break statistic is $F_T=$ `r fmt(Fobs)` °C², a
`r fmt(100 * Fobs / sum(e0^2), 1)`% reduction in RSS relative to the
linear model.
`r if (year[k] == dat$Year[which.min(dat$Temperature)]) paste0("The selected year coincides with the coldest year in the record (", year[k], ", ", fmt(min(y), 2), " °C). A continuous hinge fits a trough-shaped mean, so the least-squares kink tends to be drawn towards a pronounced local minimum, and a single extreme year can pull the estimated date towards itself. The sensitivity analysis at the end of this section therefore re-estimates the break without this year.") else ""`

Substantively, a turning point in the mid-nineteenth century is
consistent with the conventional dating of the end of the Little Ice Age
in the European Alps, where many glaciers reached their last maximum
extent around 1850 (Matthews and Briffa, 2005). This agreement is
suggestive only: a single station cannot establish a regional climate
transition.

The fitted broken trend is

$$\widehat y_i = `r fmt(coef(m1)[1])` + (`r fmt(coef(m1)[2])`)\,t_i
+ (`r fmt(coef(m1)[3])`)\,(t_i-t_{\widehat k})_+,$$

where $t_i=(\mathrm{Year}_i-1850)/10$ and
$t_{\widehat k}=(`r year[k]`-1850)/10$.
`r if (year[k] >= 1850) "Because the estimated break does not precede 1850, the hinge is zero in 1850 and the intercept is the fitted broken-trend temperature in 1850, which gives it the same interpretation as the linear-model intercept." else "Because the estimated break precedes 1850, the hinge is already positive in 1850; the intercept is the extrapolated pre-break line in 1850, not the fitted temperature."`
The pre-break slope is `r fmt(coef(m1)[2])`, the change in slope is
`r fmt(coef(m1)[3])`, and the post-break slope is
`r fmt(sum(coef(m1)[2:3]))` °C per decade.

Selecting the best date improves the fit by construction. Under
$H_0:\delta=0$ the break date is not identified, and a conventional
fixed-date test would ignore the search. At this stage the date is
therefore only the best-fitting location, not evidence that a break is
present; that question requires calibrating the entire selection
procedure under the no-break null.

## Choice of bootstrap procedures

**Why bootstrap inference.** Under $H_0:\delta=0$ the break date is not
identified, so $F_T$, which maximises the fit improvement over all
candidate dates, does not follow a standard $F$ or $\chi^2$
distribution. No closed-form finite-sample distribution is available,
and asymptotic critical values would have to be adapted to the trending
design, the unequal spacing and the dependent errors. The bootstrap
approximates the null distribution of the entire procedure, including
the date search, by resampling.

**Which bootstrap.** Section 3 found evidence of positive serial
dependence (Monte Carlo DW p = `r fmt(dwp)`), while BP did not reject
homoskedasticity against a linear variance trend (conventional p =
`r fmt(bpp)`). This non-rejection does not establish constant variance,
and the usual BP p-value does not adjust for serial dependence. The
primary procedure must therefore preserve serial dependence. We adopt
the dependent wild bootstrap (DWB; Shao, 2010). It preserves short-range dependence through
correlated multipliers and keeps each observation's own residual
magnitude. Unlike a block bootstrap, it handles unequally spaced
observations directly: the multiplier correlation decays with calendar
distance, so no block has to straddle the 1981–2009 gap.

Two secondary procedures provide a sensitivity analysis and together
form a controlled comparison. The IID residual bootstrap preserves
neither dependence nor observation-specific variance. The independent
wild bootstrap (Wu, 1986; Liu, 1988) preserves observation-specific
variance but not dependence. It is included as a variance-robust
sensitivity check: BP non-rejection against a linear variance trend
does not rule out other variance patterns. Comparing the IID residual
and wild bootstraps assesses sensitivity to the treatment of
observation-specific variance; comparing the wild bootstrap and the
DWB assesses sensitivity to the treatment of serial dependence.

**Restricted residuals and the role of the bandwidth.** All procedures
resample residuals from the null (linear) model and generate samples
around the fitted null mean. This targets $H_0$ but does not guarantee
accurate finite-sample size. If the trend changes, these restricted
residuals may contain an unmodelled kink as a slow, low-frequency
pattern. Retaining more of this structure at longer DWB bandwidths may
raise bootstrap critical values and reduce power. This is a possible
mechanism, not a guarantee: p-values need not increase monotonically
with bandwidth. Using residuals from the broken-trend fit while still
generating samples around the null mean would give a different
calibration. Its effects on size and power require a separate comparison
and are not established here.

**Bandwidth.** The primary bandwidth $\ell=6$ years follows the common
$n^{1/3}$ rate ($n^{1/3}=$ `r fmt(n^(1/3), 2)`). Under the exponential
kernel used below, it implies a multiplier correlation of
$\exp(-1/6)\approx 0.85$ between consecutive years, $\exp(-1)\approx
0.37$ at six years and about $0.14$ at twelve years. The residual
autocorrelation in Section 3 is positive but moderate at short lags
(calendar lag-one autocorrelation `r fmt(acf_gap$acf[2], 2)`), so a
six-year kernel covers the short-range dependence without reaching
deeply into the low-frequency trend component. The bandwidths $\ell=3$
and $\ell=12$ are reported as sensitivity checks.

## Bootstrap error generators

The IID residual bootstrap samples centered residuals with replacement.
It targets independent, identically distributed errors. The independent
wild bootstrap multiplies each residual by an independent Rademacher
sign, retaining its location-specific squared magnitude but removing
serial dependence.

The primary dependent wild bootstrap (DWB) uses correlated Gaussian
multipliers:

$$w_1\sim N(0,1),\quad a_i=\exp[-(s_i-s_{i-1})/\ell],\quad
w_i=a_iw_{i-1}+\sqrt{1-a_i^2}z_i,$$

where $z_i$ are independent standard Gaussians. This gives
$\operatorname{Cov}(w_i,w_j)=\exp(-|s_i-s_j|/\ell)$. Using actual
calendar gaps weakens multiplier dependence across missing years without
imputing temperatures. The multiplier correlation is a chosen dependence
approximation, not a fitted error autocorrelation.

Residuals are centered and multiplied by $\sqrt{n/(n-p)}$: $p=2$ for the
linear null and $p=3$ for the fitted broken alternative. This offsets
residual shrinkage from estimating the linear coefficients. The primary
bandwidth is six years, approximately $\operatorname{round}(n^{1/3})$.

```{r dependent-wild-weights}
dwb_weights <- function(design, B, ell = round(design$n^(1/3))) {
  stopifnot(B >= 1L, ell > 0)
  w <- matrix(rnorm(design$n * B), nrow = design$n, ncol = B)
  a <- exp(-diff(design$year) / ell)
  for (i in 2L:design$n)
    w[i, ] <- a[i - 1L] * w[i - 1L, ] + sqrt(1 - a[i - 1L]^2) * w[i, ]
  w
}
```

```{r bootstrap-error-generator}
bootstrap_errors <- function(e, year, B, method, ell = 6, df = 2) {
  n <- length(e)
  stopifnot(length(year) == n, n > df, all(is.finite(e)),
            all(is.finite(year)), B >= 1L,
            length(method) == 1L, method %in% c("iid", "wild", "dwb"))
  e <- (e - mean(e)) * sqrt(n / (n - df))
  switch(method,
    iid = matrix(sample(e, n * B, replace = TRUE), nrow = n),
    wild = e * matrix(2L * sample.int(2L, n * B, replace = TRUE) - 3L,
                      nrow = n),
    dwb = e * dwb_weights(list(n = n, year = year), B, ell))
}
```

## Bootstrap algorithms

### Algorithm A: bootstrap test of the no-break null

All three procedures share the same null-imposed generation step and
differ only in how $e_i^*$ is drawn. Let $\widehat y_{0i}$ and
$\widehat e_{0i}$ denote the fitted values and residuals of the linear
(no-break) null model `m0`, estimated by OLS on the full observed
sample.

1.  **Model estimated under the null.**
    $y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1 t_i+\varepsilon_i$ is refit by OLS on the
    observed data; $\widehat y_{0i}$ and $\widehat e_{0i}$ are held
    fixed across every bootstrap replication and every procedure.
2.  **Residuals/innovations resampled.** All three procedures resample
    the null-model residuals $\widehat e_{0i}$ themselves; DWB reweights
    them with a dependent multiplier rather than drawing a fresh
    independent sample.
3.  **Centering/rescaling.** In `bootstrap_errors()`, residuals are
    first centered, $\widehat e_{0i}-\bar{\widehat e}_0$, then inflated
    by $\sqrt{n/(n-p)}$ with $p=2$ (two null parameters) to offset the
    standard OLS shrinkage of residual variance, before any resampling
    is applied.
4.  **Generating** $y_1^*,\dots,y_n^*$.
    - *IID residual*:
      $e^*=\text{sample}(\widehat e_0,\ \text{replace}=TRUE)$.
    - *Independent wild*: $e_i^*=\widehat e_{0i}\cdot\xi_i$,
      $\xi_i\overset{iid}{\sim}\{-1,+1\}$ equiprobable (Rademacher).
    - *Dependent wild (DWB)*: $e_i^*=\widehat e_{0i}\cdot w_i$, with
      $w_i$ a mean-zero, unit-variance Gaussian sequence,
      $\operatorname{Cov}(w_i,w_j)
      =\exp(-|s_i-s_j|/\ell)$ built from actual calendar years $s_i$
      (`dwb_weights()`), $\ell=6$ for the primary specification.
    - In every case $y_i^*=\widehat y_{0i}+e_i^*$; because the null mean
      lies in the space spanned by the projected-out regressors, the
      break statistic computed from $e^*$ alone equals the one computed
      from $y^*$, so the code operates directly on $e^*$ for speed.
5.  **Computing** $F_T^*$, the critical value and the $p$-value. For
    every bootstrap draw, `break_statistics()` reruns the *entire* break
    search over all admissible dates and returns
    $F_T^*=RSS_0^*-\min_{T_c\in\Lambda}RSS_1^*(T_c)$ — the date is
    reselected in each replication, never held fixed at $\widehat T_1$.
    The empirical 95% critical value is the type-1 sample quantile of
    $F_{T}^{*(1)},\dots,
    F_{T}^{*(B)}$, and the $p$-value uses the finite-$B$ correction
    $p=\bigl(1+\#\{b:F_{T,b}^*\ge F_T\}\bigr)/(B+1)$.
6.  **Preserving dependence/heteroskedasticity.** IID residual bootstrap
    preserves neither. Independent wild preserves each observation's own
    residual magnitude (hence any heteroskedasticity in
    $\widehat e_{0i}^2$) but destroys serial dependence, since $\xi_i$
    is independent across $i$. DWB preserves both: $w_i$ has variance 1,
    so $e_i^{*2}$ keeps the same conditional scale as
    $\widehat e_{0i}^2$, while $\operatorname{Cov}(w_i,
    w_j)\neq 0$ for nearby calendar years reproduces the short-range
    positive serial dependence flagged by the Section 3 Durbin–Watson
    test.

| Element | IID residual | Independent wild | Dependent wild (primary) |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| Null model | linear trend `m0` | same | same |
| Resampled quantity | centered/rescaled $\widehat e_0$ | same, sign-flipped | same, Gaussian-multiplier-weighted |
| Centering/rescaling | mean 0, $\times\sqrt{n/(n-2)}$ | same | same |
| $y^*$ generator | $\widehat y_0+\text{sample}(\widehat e_0)$ | $\widehat y_0+\widehat e_0\,\xi$ | $\widehat y_0+\widehat e_0\,w$ |
| $F_T^*$, critical value, $p$-value | reselect break; type-1 quantile; $(1+\#\{\cdot\})/(B{+}1)$ | same | same |
| Preserves dependence? | No | No | Yes ($\ell=6$ calendar years) |
| Preserves heteroskedasticity? | No | Yes | Yes |

### Algorithm B: bootstrap confidence intervals for the slopes

The intervals use the primary DWB only and generate data under the
fitted broken-trend alternative (Davison and Hinkley, 1997, ch. 5):

1.  **Model estimated.** Fit the broken-trend model at $\widehat T_1$,
    giving fitted values $\widehat y_{1i}$, residuals $\widehat e_{1i}$
    and slope estimates
    $\widehat\theta=(\widehat\beta,\ \widehat\beta+\widehat\delta)$.
    Compute calendar-time HAC standard errors
    $s=(s_{\mathrm{pre}},s_{\mathrm{post}})$ as described below.
2.  **Centring and rescaling.** Centre $\widehat e_{1i}$ and multiply by
    $\sqrt{n/(n-3)}$, reflecting the three regression coefficients.
3.  **Bootstrap samples.** For $b=1,\ldots,B$ with $B=$ `r B_ci`, draw
    DWB multipliers $w^{(b)}$ with $\ell=6$ and set
    $y^{*(b)}_i=\widehat y_{1i}+\widehat e_{1i}\,w_i^{(b)}$.
4.  **Re-estimation.** For each $y^{*(b)}$, repeat the entire break
    search over $\Lambda$, re-estimate the model at the reselected date
    $\widehat T_1^{*(b)}$, and record $\widehat\theta^{*(b)}$ and its
    HAC standard errors $s^{*(b)}$, computed exactly as $s$.
5.  **Intervals.** The percentile interval is
    $[q_{0.025}(\widehat\theta^*),\ q_{0.975}(\widehat\theta^*)]$. The
    percentile-$t$ interval uses
    $t^{*(b)}=(\widehat\theta^{*(b)}-\widehat\theta)/s^{*(b)}$ and is
    $[\widehat\theta-q_{0.975}(t^*)\,s,\ \widehat\theta-q_{0.025}(t^*)\,s]$.
6.  **Dependence and heteroskedasticity.** As in Algorithm A, the DWB
    multipliers preserve short-range dependence and observation-specific
    variance. Re-selecting the date in step 4 carries break-date
    uncertainty into the slope intervals.

## Bootstrap test of the no-break null

For a break test, bootstrap samples must impose the no-break null. Fit
the linear model, generate $e_i^*$ from its residuals, and form
$y_i^*=\widehat y_{0i}+e_i^*$. Refit the null and search every
admissible break in each draw. Because the linear mean lies in the
projected-out space, evaluating the statistic on $e^*$ alone is
algebraically identical and faster.

The 95% critical value uses the type-1 empirical quantile. The corrected
upper-tail probability is

$$p=\frac{1+\sum_{b=1}^B\mathbf 1\{F_{T,b}^*\ge F_T\}}{B+1}.$$

The null is rejected at the 5% level when $p\le 0.05$. The function
below implements Algorithm A and is also used in the simulation study of
Section 5; for the empirical application, the subsequent chunk stores
all bootstrap statistics for plotting.

```{r bootstrap-test-function}
bootstrap_break <- function(y, design, B = 999L,
                            methods = c("iid", "wild", "dwb"),
                            seed = NULL, ell = round(design$n^(1/3)),
                            level = 0.05, keep_statistics = FALSE) {
  B <- as.integer(B)
  stopifnot(B >= 1L, level > 0, level < 1,
            length(methods) > 0, all(methods %in% c("iid", "wild", "dwb")),
            !anyDuplicated(methods))
  if (!is.null(seed)) set.seed(seed)
  observed <- fit_break(y, design)
  # Null-restricted residuals enforce the hypothesis in every bootstrap draw.
  # Degrees-of-freedom correction offsets shrinkage from estimating two terms.
  e <- observed$null_residuals
  results <- vector("list", length(methods)); names(results) <- methods
  for (method in methods) {
    boot_errors <- bootstrap_errors(e, design$year, B, method, ell, df = 2)
    # Adding the fitted null trend leaves this residual-projection statistic
    # unchanged, so computing directly from bootstrap errors is exact.
    Fstar <- break_statistics(boot_errors, design)$F
    p <- (1 + sum(Fstar >= observed$F)) / (B + 1)
    result <- list(method = method, F = observed$F, p_value = p,
                   critical = unname(quantile(Fstar, 1 - level, type = 1)),
                   reject = p <= level, B = B, level = level,
                   ell = if (method == "dwb") ell else NA_real_)
    if (keep_statistics) result$statistics <- Fstar
    results[[method]] <- result
  }
  list(observed = observed, results = results)
}
```

```{r empirical-bootstrap-tests}
methods <- c("iid", "wild", "dwb")

btests <- list()

draws <- list()

for (j in seq_along(methods)) {
    set.seed(seed + 100L + j)
    err <- bootstrap_errors(e0, year, B_test, method = methods[j], ell = 6, df = 2)
    fs <- break_statistics(err, design)$F
    draws[[methods[j]]] <- fs
    btests[[j]] <- data.frame(method = methods[j], ell = ifelse(methods[j] == "dwb", 6, NA), 
        B = B_test, statistic = Fobs, critical95 = quantile(fs, 0.95, type = 1, names = FALSE), 
        p_value = (1 + sum(fs >= Fobs))/(B_test + 1), exceedances = sum(fs >= Fobs))
}

for (ell in c(3L, 12L)) {
    set.seed(seed + 200L + ell)
    err <- bootstrap_errors(e0, year, B_test, method = "dwb", ell = ell, df = 2)
    fs <- break_statistics(err, design)$F
    btests[[length(btests) + 1]] <- data.frame(method = "dwb", ell = ell, B = B_test, statistic = Fobs, 
        critical95 = quantile(fs, 0.95, type = 1, names = FALSE), p_value = (1 + sum(fs >= 
            Fobs))/(B_test + 1), exceedances = sum(fs >= Fobs))
}

btests <- do.call(rbind, btests)

write_csv(btests, "tables/bootstrap_tests.csv")

```

```{r bootstrap-test-table}
bootstrap_table <- btests
bootstrap_table$Procedure <- c("IID residual", "Independent wild", "Dependent wild: ell=6",
                               "Dependent wild: ell=3", "Dependent wild: ell=12")
bootstrap_table$Decision <- ifelse(bootstrap_table$p_value <= .05, "Reject", "Do not reject")
knitr::kable(bootstrap_table[, c("Procedure", "B", "statistic", "critical95", "p_value", "Decision")],
             digits = 4, caption = "Unknown-break tests and dependent-wild bandwidth sensitivity")
```

Each procedure uses `r B_test` bootstrap replications. The primary DWB
with $\ell=6$ gives $p=$
`r fmt(btests$p_value[btests$method == "dwb" & !is.na(btests$ell) & btests$ell == 6])`,
`r if (btests$p_value[btests$method == "dwb" & !is.na(btests$ell) & btests$ell == 6] <= 0.05) "which rejects the no-break null at the 5% level" else "which does not reject the no-break null at the 5% level"`.
With $\ell=3$ the p-value is
`r fmt(btests$p_value[btests$method == "dwb" & !is.na(btests$ell) & btests$ell == 3])`,
and with $\ell=12$ it is
`r fmt(btests$p_value[btests$method == "dwb" & !is.na(btests$ell) & btests$ell == 12])`.
The p-values increase with bandwidth in these runs. The possible
restricted-residual mechanism discussed above is one explanation, but
this pattern is not a general monotonicity property of the DWB.
`r if (btests$p_value[btests$method == "dwb" & !is.na(btests$ell) & btests$ell == 6] <= 0.05 && btests$p_value[btests$method == "dwb" & !is.na(btests$ell) & btests$ell == 12] > 0.05 && btests$p_value[btests$method == "dwb" & !is.na(btests$ell) & btests$ell == 12] <= 0.10) "The ell = 12 result lies just above the 5% threshold. The conclusion at the conventional level is therefore bandwidth-sensitive, and the evidence for a break is better described as moderate than as decisive." else if (btests$p_value[btests$method == "dwb" & !is.na(btests$ell) & btests$ell == 6] <= 0.05 && btests$p_value[btests$method == "dwb" & !is.na(btests$ell) & btests$ell == 12] > 0.10) "The longer bandwidth does not reject, so the conclusion at the conventional level depends on the bandwidth." else ""`

If the no-break null is not rejected under a given specification,
$\widehat T_1=$ `r year[k]` cannot be read as an identified break point
under that specification. The search always returns *some* date, because
it is defined as an arg-min over $\Lambda$, but a date obtained
alongside an unrejected test is a descriptive optimum of this sample,
not evidence that the population trend changed there. The fitted broken
trend is then one flexible descriptive fit nested against the linear
trend, not a confirmed two-regime model.

The IID residual and independent wild bootstraps give p-values of
`r fmt(btests$p_value[1])` and `r fmt(btests$p_value[2])`.
`r if (all(btests$exceedances[1:2] == 0)) "Neither produced a single bootstrap statistic as large as the observed one, so both p-values equal the smallest attainable value 1/(B+1). This reflects finite simulation resolution, not a zero tail probability or a confidence bound on the underlying tail probability." else ""`
Both procedures reject at the 5% level, but their common rejection
decision does not establish that observation-specific variance is
unimportant. Their identical minimum p-values cannot resolve differences
below the simulation resolution. The contrast between these two
procedures and the DWB shows that the
evidence depends on how serial dependence is treated. Because the
independent procedures ignore the dependence detected in Section 3,
their smaller p-values do not override the primary calibration; Section
5 shows that such procedures over-reject when errors are autocorrelated.

```{r bootstrap_null-plot, fig.cap="Null bootstrap distributions under the three primary procedures; the dashed line marks the observed RSS reduction.", out.width="100%"}
plot_pair("bootstrap_null", function() {
    setup()
    dd <- lapply(draws, density)
    xmax <- max(Fobs, sapply(draws, quantile, 0.99))
    plot(dd[[1]], xlim = c(0, xmax * 1.05), col = gray, lwd = 2, xlab = "Maximum RSS reduction (degrees C squared)", 
        ylab = "Bootstrap density", main = "")
    lines(dd[[2]], col = navy, lwd = 2)
    lines(dd[[3]], col = teal, lwd = 2)
    abline(v = Fobs, col = rust, lwd = 2, lty = 2)
    legend("topright", c("IID residual", "Independent wild", "Dependent wild", "Observed"), col = c(gray, 
        navy, teal, rust), lty = c(1, 1, 1, 2), lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
}, 8, 4.3)

knitr::include_graphics(file.path(artifact_root, "figures/bootstrap_null.png"))

```

## Estimated broken trend in light of the test

At $\widehat T_1=$ `r year[k]`, the estimated pre-break trend is
$\widehat\beta=$ `r fmt(coef(m1)[2])` °C per decade, the estimated
change in trend is $\widehat\delta=$ `r fmt(coef(m1)[3])` °C per decade,
and the estimated post-break trend is $\widehat\beta+\widehat\delta=$
`r fmt(sum(coef(m1)[2:3]))` °C per decade
(`r fmt(10 * sum(coef(m1)[2:3]), 2)` °C per century). Over the
`r max(year) - year[k]` years from the estimated break to the end of the
record, the post-break slope implies a fitted warming of about
`r fmt(sum(coef(m1)[2:3]) * (max(year) - year[k]) / 10, 2)` °C, compared
with `r fmt(beta1_hat * (max(year) - year[k]) / 10, 2)` °C implied by
the single linear trend over the same period.

Two statements must be kept apart. The first is descriptive: among all
continuous one-break trends, the one with a kink at `r year[k]` fits
best, and it describes the record as
`r if (coef(m1)[2] < 0) "slight cooling" else "slight warming"` followed
by clearer warming. The second is inferential: whether the data provide
evidence that the trend changed at all. That question is answered by the
bootstrap test above, which
`r if (btests$p_value[btests$method == "dwb" & !is.na(btests$ell) & btests$ell == 6] <= 0.05) "supports a break under the primary procedure, subject to the bandwidth sensitivity noted there" else "does not support a break at the 5% level under the primary procedure"`.
The estimated slopes and date are meaningful as a description regardless
of the test outcome, but they can be read as an estimate of a structural
change only to the extent that the test supports one. The uncertainty of
the slopes is quantified next.

## Bootstrap confidence intervals for the slopes

### Studentisation: calendar-time HAC standard errors

The percentile-$t$ interval requires a standard error in every bootstrap
sample, so that the studentised statistic $t^*$ is approximately
pivotal, which typically makes the interval more accurate than the
percentile interval. Because the errors are serially dependent,
conventional OLS standard errors would misstate the sampling
variability, so we use a heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation
consistent (HAC) estimator in the spirit of Newey and West (1987),
adapted to calendar time.

Confidence intervals generate data under the **fitted broken
alternative**, rather than the null. Each draw repeats the date search
and re-estimates both slopes. Percentile intervals use the bootstrap
slope quantiles. Studentized percentile-$t$ intervals also recompute a
standard error in every draw.

The local Jacobian contains the date derivative:

$$J_i=[1,x_i,(x_i-\tau)_+,-\widehat\delta\mathbf 1(x_i>\tau)],\qquad \tau=x_{\widehat k}.$$

For numerical stability, the fourth column is rescaled to the indicator
$\mathbf 1(x_i>\tau)$. With a nonzero slope change, this does not change
the covariance of the first three coefficients. The pre- and post-break
contrasts are $(0,1,0,0)$ and $(0,1,1,0)$.

The calendar Bartlett kernel is $K_{ij}=\max\{1-|s_i-s_j|/7,0\}$. Only
observed pairs exactly one to six calendar years apart enter the lag
terms. The finite-sample multiplier is $n/(n-4)$, counting the local
date parameter as well as the three regression coefficients. This is a
local HAC approximation, and weak date identification can limit
coverage.

```{r calendar-hac-standard-errors}
calendar_hac_se <- function(year, X, e, L=6) {
  n <- nrow(X); p <- ncol(X); A <- solve(crossprod(X))
  C <- cbind(c(0,1,0,0),c(0,1,1,0))
  influence <- (X %*% A %*% C)*as.numeric(e)
  v <- colSums(influence^2)
  for (lag in seq_len(L)) {
    j <- match(year+lag,year); i <- which(!is.na(j))
    if(length(i)) v <- v+2*(1-lag/(L+1))*colSums(influence[i,,drop=FALSE]*influence[j[i],,drop=FALSE])
  }
  sqrt(pmax(v*n/(n-p),.Machine$double.eps))
}
```

### Bootstrap samples under the alternative

The alternative residual scaling uses three linear coefficients, while
the local sandwich uses four parameters including the date; these
corrections serve different roles. The bootstrap loop records reselected
dates, slope estimates and their HAC standard errors, making the
reported intervals independently reconstructible.

```{r confidence-interval-refits}
# Alternative bootstrap: both break location and slope estimates are refitted.
set.seed(seed+301L)
err<-bootstrap_errors(e1,year,B_ci,method="dwb",ell=6,df=3)
Ystar<-as.numeric(fitted(m1))+err
coefstar<-sestar<-matrix(NA_real_,B_ci,2); breakyears<-integer(B_ci)
seobs<-calendar_hac_se(year,cbind(X1,as.numeric(x>x[k])),e1)
for (b in seq_len(B_ci)) {
  ff<-fit_break(Ystar[,b],design); kk<-ff$index
  XX<-cbind(1,x,pmax(0,x-x[kk])); fit<-lm.fit(XX,Ystar[,b])
  coefstar[b,]<-c(fit$coefficients[2],sum(fit$coefficients[2:3]))
  sestar[b,]<-calendar_hac_se(year,cbind(XX,as.numeric(x>x[kk])),fit$residuals)
  breakyears[b]<-year[kk]
}
```

For either slope $\theta$, the percentile interval is
$[q_{.025}(\widehat\theta^*),q_{.975}(\widehat\theta^*)]$. For the
studentized interval, calculate

$$t^*=\frac{\widehat\theta^*-\widehat\theta}{s^*},\qquad
[\widehat\theta-q_{.975}(t^*)s,\ \widehat\theta-q_{.025}(t^*)s].$$

CI quantiles use R's interpolated type 7. Notice the reversed quantile
order in the studentized endpoints. Holding the selected date fixed in
bootstrap samples would omit part of slope uncertainty.

```{r construct-confidence-intervals}
tstar<-sweep(sweep(coefstar,2,theta,"-"),c(1,2),sestar,"/")
cis<-do.call(rbind,lapply(1:2,function(j){
  pc<-quantile(coefstar[,j],c(.025,.975),type=7,names=FALSE)
  qt<-quantile(tstar[,j],c(.975,.025),type=7,names=FALSE)
  pt<-theta[j]-seobs[j]*qt
  data.frame(parameter=c("pre","post")[j],estimate=unname(theta[j]),hac_se=unname(seobs[j]),
             type=c("percentile","percentile_t"),lower=c(pc[1],pt[1]),upper=c(pc[2],pt[2]),B=B_ci)
}))
write_csv(cis,"tables/confidence_intervals.csv")
knitr::kable(cis, digits = 4, caption = "Nominal 95% intervals in degrees C per decade")
```

`r if (all(cis$lower[cis$parameter == "pre"] <= 0 & cis$upper[cis$parameter == "pre"] >= 0)) "Both pre-break intervals contain zero. Statistically, the data are compatible with no trend before the break; substantively, the negative point estimate does not establish early cooling." else "At least one pre-break interval excludes zero."`
`r if (all(cis$lower[cis$parameter == "post"] > 0)) "Both post-break intervals lie entirely above zero. Statistically, a zero post-break slope is not supported within the broken-trend model; substantively, this indicates sustained warming at this station after the estimated break." else "At least one post-break interval contains zero."`
These intervals are conditional on the broken-trend specification and do
not by themselves test whether a break exists. Their coverage has not
been evaluated by simulation (Section 5 studies test size and power
only), and the percentile-$t$ intervals rely on a local HAC
approximation, which may be less accurate where the date is weakly
identified.

```{r slope_intervals-plot, fig.cap="Percentile and percentile-t intervals; the vertical reference marks zero slope.", out.width="100%"}
plot_pair("slope_intervals", function() {
    setup()
    par(mar = c(4.2, 8.3, 1.5, 1))
    yy <- 4:1
    cols <- rep(c(navy, teal), 2)
    plot(cis$estimate, yy, xlim = range(c(cis$lower, cis$upper, 0)), ylim = c(0.5, 4.5), 
        yaxt = "n", xlab = "Temperature trend (degrees C per decade)", ylab = "", pch = 16, 
        col = cols)
    segments(cis$lower, yy, cis$upper, yy, col = cols, lwd = 2)
    abline(v = 0, lty = 3, col = gray)
    axis(2, at = yy, labels = c("Pre: percentile", "Pre: percentile-t", "Post: percentile", 
        "Post: percentile-t"), las = 1, tick = FALSE, cex.axis = 0.8)
}, 8, 3.8)

knitr::include_graphics(file.path(artifact_root, "figures/slope_intervals.png"))

```

```{r break_bootstrap_distribution-plot, fig.cap="Reselected dates across all alternative-bootstrap samples.", out.width="100%"}
plot_pair("break_bootstrap_distribution", function() {
    setup()
    hist(breakyears, breaks = seq(min(year[candidates]) - 0.5, max(year[candidates]) + 4.5, 
        by = 5), col = teal_fill, border = "white", xlab = "Reselected break year", ylab = "Bootstrap replications", 
        main = "")
    abline(v = year[k], col = navy, lwd = 2)
}, 8, 4)

```{r date-variation-summary}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Lower_date_percentile = unname(quantile(breakyears, .025)),
  Upper_date_percentile = unname(quantile(breakyears, .975)),
  Boundary_selection_percent = 100 * mean(breakyears %in% range(year[candidates]))
), digits = 2)
```

The date percentiles describe selection variability under the fitted
alternative. They are not an established 95% confidence set for a weakly
identified break date. The spread of reselected dates contributes to the
width and possible asymmetry of the slope intervals.

## Model comparison and residual diagnostics

RSS, in-sample RMSE and $R^2$ describe fit. A searched model is more
flexible, so improvement alone is not selection-adjusted evidence. The
bootstrap addresses that distinction. The broken residuals should also
be inspected rather than assuming that a new mean model removes
dependence.

```{r model-comparison}
diagnostic<-function(m,label){
  e<-resid(m); bb<-n*summary(lm(e^2~x))$r.squared
  data.frame(model=label,RSS=sum(e^2),RMSE=sqrt(mean(e^2)),R2=summary(m)$r.squared,
    adjusted_R2=summary(m)$adj.r.squared,DW=sum(diff(e)^2)/sum(e^2),
    acf1=acf(e,plot=FALSE)$acf[2],BP=bb,BP_p=pchisq(bb,1,lower.tail=FALSE))
}
dg<-rbind(diagnostic(m0,"linear"),diagnostic(m1,"broken"))
write_csv(dg,"tables/model_diagnostics.csv")
knitr::kable(dg, digits = 4, caption = "Fit measures and remaining residual dependence")
```

The reduction in RSS is `r fmt(100 * Fobs / sum(e0^2), 2)`%. RMSE falls
from `r fmt(dg$RMSE[1], 3)` to `r fmt(dg$RMSE[2], 3)` °C, and $R^2$
rises from `r fmt(dg$R2[1], 3)` to `r fmt(dg$R2[2], 3)`. Most annual
variation remains unexplained by either model.

Because the broken model estimates a break date in addition to its three
coefficients, adjusted $R^2$, which counts only three parameters,
slightly overstates its advantage. A Bayesian information criterion that
counts the date as a fourth parameter,
$\mathrm{BIC}=n\log(RSS/n)+p\log n$, equals
`r fmt(n * log(dg$RSS[1] / n) + 2 * log(n), 1)` for the linear model
($p=2$) and `r fmt(n * log(dg$RSS[2] / n) + 4 * log(n), 1)` for the
broken model ($p=4$),
`r if ((n * log(dg$RSS[2] / n) + 4 * log(n)) < (n * log(dg$RSS[1] / n) + 2 * log(n))) "so the broken trend is preferred even after this penalty" else "so the linear trend is preferred once the date is penalised"`.
Because the break date enters the model non-regularly, BIC is only a
heuristic here; the bootstrap test remains the formal comparison.

The Durbin–Watson statistic of the broken-trend residuals
(`r fmt(dg$DW[2], 3)`) is closer to two than that of the linear model
(`r fmt(dg$DW[1], 3)`), and the observation-lag ACF(1) falls from
`r fmt(dg$acf1[1], 3)` to `r fmt(dg$acf1[2], 3)`. These values are not
formally calibrated: the design now depends on the estimated date, so
the Section 3 critical values do not apply. Together with the residual
ACF below, they indicate that the kink absorbs part, but not all, of the
residual dependence, which supports using a dependence-robust bootstrap
for the slope intervals.

```{r diagnostics_broken-plot, fig.cap="Residual diagnostics after selecting the broken trend; dependence remains visible.", out.width="100%"}
plot_pair("diagnostics_broken", function() {
    par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 0.7), mgp = c(2.5, 0.7, 0),
        col.axis = axis_colour, col.lab = label_colour,
        col.main = label_colour, cex = 0.8)
    plot(year, e1, pch = 16, cex = 0.5, col = gray, xlab = "Calendar year", ylab = "Residual (degrees C)", 
        main = "Broken-trend residuals")
    abline(h = 0, col = navy, lty = 2)
    acf(e1, lag.max = 20, main = "", xlab = "Observation lag", ylab = "Autocorrelation", 
        col = navy, ci.col = teal)
    title("ACF by observation lag", line = 0.6, cex.main = 1.1)
    plot(year, e1^2, pch = 16, cex = 0.5, col = gray, xlab = "Calendar year", ylab = "Squared residual (degrees C squared)", 
        main = "Residual variance")
    lines(lowess(year, e1^2, f = 0.3), col = teal, lwd = 2)
    qqnorm(e1, pch = 16, cex = 0.5, col = gray, main = "Normal QQ plot", ylab = "Residual quantile (degrees C)")
    qqline(e1, col = teal, lwd = 2)
}, 8, 6)

knitr::include_graphics(file.path(artifact_root, "figures/diagnostics_broken.png"))

```

**Overall comparison.** Substantively, the broken trend is the more
convincing description: it replaces a single average slope with a
flat-to-cooling phase followed by warming, matches the pattern seen in
Section 2, and yields a post-break slope
`r fmt(sum(coef(m1)[2:3]) / beta1_hat, 1)` times the linear slope.
Statistically, the case is
`r if (btests$p_value[btests$method == "dwb" & !is.na(btests$ell) & btests$ell == 6] <= 0.05) "supported but not decisive" else "weak"`:
`r if ((n * log(dg$RSS[2] / n) + 4 * log(n)) < (n * log(dg$RSS[1] / n) + 2 * log(n))) "the fit improvement survives a penalty for the additional parameters" else "the fit improvement does not survive a penalty for the additional parameters"`
and the primary bootstrap test
`r if (btests$p_value[btests$method == "dwb" & !is.na(btests$ell) & btests$ell == 6] <= 0.05) "rejects" else "does not reject"`
the linear model, but the conclusion is sensitive to the dependence
bandwidth, and residual dependence remains in both models.

## Sensitivity to individual observations

Two descriptive checks omit the coldest observation in 1851 or end the
sample in 1980, excluding the four observations after the long gap. Each
check reselects the break using 15% trimming. These are point-estimate
sensitivities, not new bootstrap significance tests. Every primary
result above retains the complete supplied sample.

```{r sample-sensitivity}
# Secondary diagnostics only: retain the complete sample for every primary result.
sensitivities <- list(no_coldest = which(year != 1851), pre_gap = which(year <= 1980))

ss <- lapply(names(sensitivities), function(label) {
    ii <- sensitivities[[label]]
    fit <- fit_break(y[ii], prepare_design(year[ii]))
    xx <- (year[ii] - mean(year[ii]))/10
    mm <- lm(y[ii] ~ xx + I(pmax(0, xx - xx[fit$index])))
    data.frame(sample = label, n = length(ii), break_year = year[ii][fit$index], pre = coef(mm)[2], 
        post = sum(coef(mm)[2:3]), F = fit$F)
})

write_csv(do.call(rbind, ss), "tables/sample_sensitivity.csv")

sample_sensitivity <- read.csv("tables/sample_sensitivity.csv")

knitr::kable(sample_sensitivity, digits = 4)

```

Excluding 1851 moves the selected date to
`r sample_sensitivity$break_year[1]` and changes $F_T$ from
`r fmt(Fobs, 2)` to `r fmt(sample_sensitivity$F[1], 2)`. Ending the
sample in 1980 selects `r sample_sensitivity$break_year[2]`, with a
post-break slope of `r fmt(sample_sensitivity$post[2], 4)` °C per
decade. The estimated location of the kink is therefore not an artefact
of the coldest year alone or of the four post-gap observations, although
the coldest year does contribute to the strength of the fit. These
checks do not address unknown station history, model selection or the
missing decades.
